items.title: 9.1 Anatomy and physiology of the digestive system

source_refs.note: Chapter opening and the single topic 9.1, printed pages 202-212, as printed, with its side boxes and Figures 9.1 to 9.8 where the book prints them. The learning outcomes and exercises are not reproduced.

blocks.text: Digestion is the process by which the body breaks down food into smaller, absorbable components. Digestion is crucial for converting food into energy and raw materials required for growth, repair and maintenance of body functions. It supports the immune system, provides essential nutrients and ensures overall health. Efficient digestion prevents nutrient deficiencies, supports metabolism and maintains energy levels, making it vital for sustaining life.

The human digestive system is composed of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract and accessory digestive organs. The GI tract is a continuous tube that extends from mouth to anus. It includes oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. The accessory digestive organs include the salivary glands, liver, gallbladder and pancreas.

blocks.alt: An outline of the head and trunk showing the gut from mouth to anus: Tongue, Salivary glands, Pharynx, Oesophagus, Stomach, the Small intestine (Duodenum, Jejunum, Ileum) and the Colon (Transverse colon, Ascending colon, Descending colon), with the Cecum, Appendix, Rectum and Anus. The Liver, Gallbladder and Pancreas lie by the stomach; the Common bile duct and Pancreatic duct join the duodenum.
